### Vowels

Unrounded vowels come before the dot, rounded after it. Length: no long vowels. Nasality: no nasal vowels.

## Orthography

The house romanization in two registers: the full spelling (workbench, one letter or digraph per sound, tone marks) and the book spelling (lossy: no tone, plain vowels, and at most 2 diacritic letters kept for the whole language; one spelling per sound in every word). Allophones are spelled as their phonemes.

**Consonants:** n ‹n› · ŋ ‹ng› · t ‹t› · d ‹d› · k͡p ‹kp› · ɡ͡b ‹gb› · ʔ ‹'› · tʃ ‹ch› · s ‹s› · h ‹h› · j ‹y› · w ‹w› · l ‹l› · ȴ ‹ľ› · r ‹rr› · rʲ ‹rry›

**Vowels:** i ‹i› · iᴖ ‹iwh› · u ‹u› · uᴖ ‹uwh› · e ‹e› · eᴖ ‹ewh› · oᴖ ‹owh› · ə ‹ë› ‹e› · o̞ ‹o› · ɛ ‹ẹ› ‹e› · ɔ ‹ọ› ‹o› · a ‹a›

Tones are written over the vowel: low grave à, high acute á, rising caron ǎ, falling circumflex â (Yoruba-style).

Where two spellings are given the second is the book spelling.

## Grammar

Basic word order is VOS; it has prepositions. In the noun phrase: possessed before the possessor; noun before the adjective; noun before the demonstrative; noun before the numeral; noun before the relative clause. Overall it is head-initial.
It has no definite article, no indefinite article, no case marking on nouns, no alignment marking (subject and object are not told apart by form), no grammatical number, no gender or noun classes.
Verbs mark perfective and progressive; there are no evidentials. Negation uses a negator before the verb; yes/no questions use a verb form. Verbs agree with the subject by suffixes; not with the object.
Other features: pronouns can be dropped; an inclusive/exclusive 'we' distinction; verb reduplication; a periphrastic causative; no passive; question words left in place; a decimal counting base; a 'have' verb for possession.
Measured morphology: 13 live grammatical markers, mean bondedness 1.4 (0 free word … 3 fused), 32 paradigm cells, 7 of them with allomorphy.

### Grammar sketch

Built from the typology and the live markers above (planet/language/sentences.py); where the engine tracks no marker for a construction, the form is the word such markers commonly grow from, and the text says so. Examples are glossed by the Leipzig rules (abbreviations under Sample sentences).

**Number.** Nouns do not mark number: one noun form serves for one or many; a numeral or 'many' says how many.

**Case.** Nouns have no case marking. Subject and object are not marked apart: word order tells them. Place and company are said with the plain words 'in' (tʃa˦hi˦li˨h), 'at' (tʃa˦hi˦li˨h), 'with' (ni˨) as adpositions.

**Gender and noun classes.** There is no gender or noun class.

**Tense and aspect.** Verbs mark tense and aspect. Perfect (PRF): a prefix (i˨, from 'hold'); progressive (PROG): a prefix (la˨n, from 'at'); completive ('finish, fully') (COMPL): a separate word before the verb (di˨hsu˦˨, from 'finish'). Unmarked: past, future, habitual (left to context).

| *i˨-ha˨da˨tʃi˨tʃi˨* |
| --- |
| PRF-go |

‘(it) has gone’

| *la˨n-ha˨da˨tʃi˨tʃi˨* |
| --- |
| PROG-go |

‘(it) is going’

| *di˨hsu˦˨* | *ha˨da˨tʃi˨tʃi˨* |
| --- | --- |
| COMPL | go |

‘(it) has gone completely’

**Mood and evidentiality.** Mood markers: hortative ('let us') (HORT): a clitic before the verb (ho̞˦, from 'leave').

| *ho̞˦=ha˨da˨tʃi˨tʃi˨* |
| --- |
| HORT=go |

‘let us go’

**Person agreement.** Verbs agree with the subject: 2SG: a clitic after the verb (ɛ˦n; jɛ˦n after a front or central vowel; from 'thou'); 2PL: a clitic after the verb (ɛ˦nnɛ˨k͡p; jɛ˦nnɛ˨k͡p after a front or central vowel; from 'you'); 3PL: a clitic after the verb (u˦ᴖli˨w; ju˦ᴖli˨w after a front or central vowel; from 'they'). Subject pronouns are dropped when the marker is there. No marker yet for 1SG, 3SG, 1PL (zero).

| *ha˨da˨tʃi˨tʃi˨=jɛ˦n* |
| --- |
| go=2SG |

‘you go’

| *ha˨da˨tʃi˨tʃi˨=jɛ˦nnɛ˨k͡p* |
| --- |
| go=2PL |

‘you all go’

| *ha˨da˨tʃi˨tʃi˨=ju˦ᴖli˨w* |
| --- |
| go=3PL |

‘they go’

**Negation.** Negation uses the word for 'not' (i˦ᴖ), preverbal.

| *i˦ᴖ* | *tʃa˦* | *u˦˨* | *nu˨ᴖw* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NEG | drink | milk | 1SG |

‘I do not drink the milk.’ (sentence 6 below)

**Questions.** Yes/no questions use a marker on the verb. Question words stay where the questioned phrase would stand: who nu˨ᴖi˨u˨la˨h, what u˦, where a˨ŋu˨tʃi˨tʃn, when ɛ˨, how k͡pa˦k͡p.

| *ji˦˨h-ʔu˦h=ɛ˦n* | *u˦ᴖi˨u˨ᴖlu˨ᴖw* |
| --- | --- |
| hear-Q=2SG | thunder |

‘Do you hear the thunder?’ (sentence 4 below)

| *u˨˦ᴖhe˦jhi˦* | *u˦* | *ja˨d* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| bring | what | child |

‘What does the child bring?’ (sentence 5 below)

**Commands.** There is no imperative marker: a command is the bare verb stem, with no subject and no subject or tense marker. 'Let us ...' has a hortative marker of its own.

| *ʔo̞˦* | *e˨* |
| --- | --- |
| eat | fish |

‘Eat the fish!’ (sentence 12 below)

| *ho̞˦=ʔo̞˦* | *e˨* |
| --- | --- |
| HORT=eat | fish |

‘Let us eat the fish!’ (sentence 15 below)

**Possession.** The possessor stands after the possessed noun, with no marker. 'Having' is said with a 'have' verb ('my mother has a boat').

| *du˦* | *i˨u˨la˨h* |
| --- | --- |
| dog | man |

‘the man's dog’

| *ɛ˦j* | *lu˨ju˦ᴖe˦ᴖw* | *re˦* | *nu˨ᴖw* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| have | boat | mother | 1SG |

‘My mother has a boat.’ (sentence 7 below)

**Relative clauses.** Relative clause after the noun, introduced by the word for 'that' (as English that and German der grew from a pointing word).

| *ɛ˦w* | *ni˦n* | *tʃa˨n* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| woman | REL | dance |

‘the woman who dances’

**Copula.** There is no copula: a predicate noun stands beside its subject.

| *i˨u˨la˨h* | *ni˦n* | *ʔo̞˦nu˨d* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| man | that | merchant |

‘That man is a merchant.’ (sentence 9 below)

| *u˦ᴖe˦ᴖw* | *hi˨hu˦i˨h* |
| --- | --- |
| water | cold |

‘the water is cold’

**Pronouns.** 'We' has two forms: inclusive u˨ᴖi˦nnu˨ᴖw (you and I, the hearer among us) and exclusive ə˦˨ (we, but not you).

| *u˨ᴖi˦nnu˨ᴖw* |
| --- |
| 1PL.INCL |

‘we (you included)’

| *ə˦˨* |
| --- |
| 1PL.EXCL |

‘we (not you)’

| *ʔo̞˦* | *e˨* | *u˨ᴖi˦nnu˨ᴖw* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| eat | fish | 1PL.INCL |

‘We (you and I) eat the fish.’ (sentence 14 below)

**Reduplication.** Verbs reduplicate for an action done again and again, or by many (ITER), by copying the stem's first consonant and vowel before it.

| *ha˨-ha˨da˨tʃi˨tʃi˨* |
| --- |
| ITER-go |

‘(an action done again and again, or by many)’

| *hi˦-hi˦d* | *e˨* | *i˨u˨la˨h* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ITER-hit | fish | man |

‘The man hits the fish again and again.’ (sentence 13 below)

**Giving (two objects).** Double object: theme and recipient both unmarked.

| *we˨˦hi˦ᴖh* | *e˨* | *ja˨d* | *ɛ˦w* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| give | fish | child | woman |

‘The woman gives the child a fish.’ (sentence 11 below)

**Numerals.** Counting is decimal: numbers above ten are built from ten and the units. Twenty is u˨nnɛ˨k͡p and a hundred is ni˨dʔɛ˦u˨h.

| *u˨ᴖwn* |
| --- |
| 11 |

‘11 = 10 + 1 ('ten' and 'one')’

| *u˦ᴖwn* |
| --- |
| 15 |

‘15 = 10 + 5 ('ten' and 'five')’

| *u˨n* |
| --- |
| 30 |

‘30 = 10 × 3 ('ten' and 'three')’

**Voice and pivot.** Each clause picks one phrase as its pivot, and the verb's voice says which: actor voice (AV): a prefix that fuses with some stems (u˨ᴖw, from 'do').

| *u˨ᴖw-ʔo̞˦* | *e˨* | *i˨u˨la˨h* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AV-eat | fish | man |

‘The man eats a fish.’ (sentence 17 below)

**Linking clauses.** Complement clauses stand bare, with no complementizer.

| *ta˨˦ʔi˨h* | *i˦ᴖɡ͡b* | *du˦* | *i˨u˨la˨h* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| say | sleep | dog | man |

‘The man says that the dog sleeps.’ (sentence 16 below)

**Demonstratives.** Demonstratives count three distances: 'this' ni˨n (near), 'that' ni˦n (further) and a far one, a separate word after the noun phrase (ni˦nn, from 'that'; 'that' with a place word grown onto it, as English 'that there' became 'yon').

| *du˦* | *ni˨n* |
| --- | --- |
| dog | this |

‘this dog’

| *du˦* | *ni˦n* |
| --- | --- |
| dog | that |

‘that dog’

| *du˦* | *ni˦nn* |
| --- | --- |
| dog | DIST |

‘that dog over there (yon)’

**Comparison.** An 'exceed' comparison: 'A is big, exceeds B', with the verb for 'climb' (as Yoruba ju 'exceed', Thai kwaa 'cross over').

| *i˨u˨la˨h* | *k͡pu˦hu˦k͡pe˨h* | *o˦ᴖ* | *du˦* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| man | big | exceed | dog |

‘The man is bigger than the dog.’ (sentence 20 below)

Counting base: decimal. Several numerals began as other words: two < 'pair'; five < 'hold'; eight = 'four + two'; nine = 'ten + one'; twenty = 'ten two'; hundred = 'twenty five'.

## Names of people and places

**Naming tradition.** Given names are a short sentence about the birth run together (as Yoruba *Babatunde* 'father has returned'); the byname is an epithet after the name. The tradition goes back to the aarakocra proto-language.

| name | IPA | meaning | | etymology |
\|---\|---\|---\|---\|---\|
| **Uwhhehuwhy** | /u˨˦ᴖhe˦hu˨ᴖj/ | 'the rain came' | old | Uwhhehuwhy 'the rain came': uwhheh 'come' + uwhy 'rain'; an old name, coined in d292 4.0 kyr ago as Uwhhehuwhy |
| **Huwhyedi** | /hu˨ᴖjɛ˨di˨/ | 'the people sing' | old | Huwhyedi 'the people sing': huwhyed 'sing' + iulahad 'people'; an old name, coined in d292 4.0 kyr ago as Huwhyediu |
| **Dihsungasuwhs** | /di˨hsu˦˨ŋa˨su˨ᴖs/ | 'the war is over' | old | Dihsungasuwhs 'the war is over': dihsu 'finish' + ngasuwhssuwh 'war'; an old name, coined in d292 4.0 kyr ago as Dihsungasuwhs |
| **Suyi'un** | /su˨ji˦ʔu˦n/ | 'the sun rose' | new | Suyi'un 'the sun rose': suyihusunun 'rise' + un 'sun'; coined from today's words |
| **Urr** | /ʔu˦r/ | 'mother laughed' | new | Urr 'mother laughed': u 'laugh' + rre 'mother'; coined from today's words |
| **Ti'ichkpon** | /ti˦ʔi˦tʃk͡po̞˨n/ | 'God knows' | new | Ti'ichkpon 'God knows': ti'ich 'know' + kponkparryikp 'god'; coined from today's words |
| **Uwhhehuwhy Hidleh** | /u˨˦ᴖhe˦hu˨ᴖj hi˦dle˨h/ | 'the rain came, the black' | epithet | hidleh 'black', a byname |
| **Huwhyedi Hidleh** | /hu˨ᴖjɛ˨di˨ hi˦dle˨h/ | 'the people sing, the black' | epithet | hidleh 'black', a byname |

**Settlements.** **Suwhyiwinhuy** /su˨ᴖji˨wi˨nhu˨j/ (village, 511): 'the black field'; named by the human (d561.1) who founded it lately, kept as heard.

## Gods and liturgy

**Faith.** The fire schism of the aarakocra of the north of Sothasor, founded 14 kyr ago ago, held by 6 languages.

| god of mountain and forest | **In** | /i˦n/ | 'the lord' | — |
| god of sky and storm | **Iy** | /i˨j/ | 'the one who sees' | — |
| god of sea and rain | **Igbnauwhy** | /i˨ɡ͡bna˨u˦ᴖj/ | 'River' | Igbnauwhy (aarakocra 34) |
| god of hunt and fertility | **Kpu** | /k͡pu˦/ | 'chief of the hunt' | Kpule (aarakocra 34) |

How the first name came about: 'the lord' (a title in place of the name (the old name avoided); it replaced the old name u˨ᴖw 'the one who stands') in d292, 5 kyr ago.

**Liturgy.** The faith's rites are kept in the aarakocra speech of aarakocra 8 as it was 5 kyr ago ago, frozen since (as Latin, Sanskrit or Ge'ez are).

## Sample sentences

Built from this language's own words, word order, markers and agreement (planet/language/sentences.py). Each has the form line (‘-’ an affix boundary, ‘=’ a clitic boundary), a morpheme-by-morpheme gloss, the free translation, then the whole sentence in IPA (after the simple joining rules: a glide between two vowels, a nasal taking the place of a following stop) and in the book spelling. Nothing here is attested speech; it is what the grammar data implies.

**(1)** ‘The woman sees the dog.’

| *ra˨* | *du˦* | *ɛ˦w* |
| --- | --- | --- |

Abbreviations: 1 first person; 2 second person; AV actor voice (the doer is the pivot); COMPL completive ('finish, fully'); HORT hortative ('let us'); INCL inclusive (you among us); ITER iterative (reduplication); NEG negation; PL plural; PRF perfect; Q question particle; REL relativizer; SG singular.

## Texts

Each sentence in four lines: the book spelling, the IPA with its morph breaks, the gloss, and the English.

### A fable: The Bird and the Fish

One fixed short fable, told in every language as August Schleicher told his in Proto-Indo-European (1868), so that the same text shows what sound change and grammar change did. English: A bird sat in a tree. The bird saw a fish in the water. The bird said: “Come! I will give you a good seed.” The fish said: “I do not eat seeds. You will eat me.” The fish did not come. The bird ate the seed.

### A myth: What the gods hold (the fire schism of the aarakocra of the north of Sothasor)
